In relation to that and this point he wanted to make about KLA being in Djakovica in April he referred to their exhibit 6D1637, 1638, and 1639. We would direct you to their documents themselves which contain disclaimers about the information contained in there. 6D1637 and 6D1639 both contain the disclaimer that says: "Much of the information cannot be confirmed." And 6D1638 says that the information contained was gleaned from KLA sources. One other reference to the Pristina folks, Mr. Ivetic makes reference to the term "identity cleansing." And he says there was no information that the people sent out to Djeneral Jankovic had their personal documents destroyed. I guess he was saying Ms. Bala, and Mr. Kabashi, K-62, and 63, none of them testified that they had their personal documents destroyed, but I would direct you to the statement of Ms. Bala in Exhibit P2262, page 8, where she talked about at the border at Djeneral Jankovic, seeing the border police take documents from 100 men and later other men told her that they had had their identity documents taken as well. With regard to Sadije Sadiku you'll remember the young woman in the wheelchair who testified here. He says the Prosecution cannot change her testimony and change the fact that this testimony was shown to be false from the official response from the government that she did not have previously issued identity documents. I guess that presupposes she said that her identity document was taken. I believe her testimony and her statement was to the effect that the group she was with had their identity documents taken away, and argues that, you know, since we were able to obtain her identity document in the year 2008 somehow rebuts our theory of the case. We say that the documents in 2008 are no reflection of the intention in 1999 and what happened then. And you'll recall that we had evidence earlier in the Defence case where it was purported that Sadije Sadiku did not exist, that there was no record regarding her, which was rebutted by evidence we obtained later in the case. There's a reference to Mr. Lukic's interview, Mr. Ivetic claims that regarding paragraph 228 of the Prosecution's brief we claim that the Joint Command issued orders for joint action and say that Lukic acknowledged this and his role was to ensure that the orders were carried out but there was no citation for that proposition as to what his role was. In the brief at paragraph 228 we say his role was to ensure that the Joint Command plans involving MUP units were carried out. There's no citation to that sentence, but in the very next sentence we say: "He would determine units needed for specific actions and task his subordinates to provide the required personnel." That's cited -- that's then footnoted in footnote 57 with a reference to Cvetic and his transcript at 8075, 8080, 8194 to 8195. And regarding paragraph 228, footnote 57, there's also a reference to Mr. Lukic's interview at pages 48 and 49 and page 72. The reference to page 72 in the interview in footnote 57 is a mistake. That should read page 77. I think 72 is a reference to his earlier statement before we merged the English and the B/C/S. And likewise, in paragraph 1013 of our brief at footnote 2448 we make a reference to Exhibit P949 and pages 35-36; that was another error in the page numbering, that should be pages 48 and 49 of the interview. Then there is an attack on the credibility of a couple of the Prosecution witnesses, particularly Shaun Byrnes and General Vasiljevic. Regarding General Vasiljevic, Mr. Ivetic mentions one of the falsehoods committed by him. At page 71 yesterday he said one falsehood that he did not get around to correcting was his that among the SAJ were persons who had a combined 150 years of jail sentences. I don't know if it's SAJ or JSO. It's actually JAS in my transcript and I'm not sure which he referred to. According to information from his service he says at the time. Unfortunately for him and the Prosecution General Dimitrijevic refuted Vasiljevic, saying that VJ intelligence had no such information. That's not quite an accurate statement of what Dimitrijevic said. He was asked if he knew about any such information and he said no. But I would note that Dimitrijevic was no longer the head of intelligence as of the start of the war and that Vasiljevic returned in late April 1999. So he had access to information at a point in time after Dimitrijevic was no longer there. Byrnes and Vasiljevic, we simply ask you to review their testimony and their statements and judge for yourself their credibility. And regarding those citations there's another one raised by Mr. Ivetic in our brief. He says the Prosecution asserted that the RDB chief in Kosovo, David Gajic, was a member of the staff and JSO commander Legija was also a commander. He says: "I ask you to note that the citation given for these assertions which gives the impression that the citations are supportive is 180 degrees counter." They cite to Joksic who spent a great deal of time negating this assertion. Your Honour, perhaps there's some possibility that Mr. Ivetic didn't read it closely, but if you'll look at that citation in the brief and the footnotes you'll see that Joksic is cited for the proposition that David Gajic was the head of the RDB in Kosovo and Legija was the commander of the JSO. The citation supporting the proposition that those two individuals were members of the MUP staff is a reference to Exhibit P1505, which is the Minister of the Interior Stojiljkovic's decision creating a MUP staff for the suppression of terrorism. So that's another instance where he got it wrong. Finally, Mr. Lukic returned to speak briefly and one point he raised was concerning the wearing of coloured ribbons and he refers to our witness Abdullah Salihu who testified that on the 29th of March there were Serb forces wearing ribbons, red, blue, and yellow. In his statement in P2255 Mr. Lukic says: "As far as members of the MUP are concerned the bands began to be worn on the 15th of April and there were never three colours," referring to Exhibit 6D237. Your Honour, you will recall we have evidence that in July 1998 the MUP were wearing ribbons for the purposes, as testified to by some of the witnesses, to identify themselves and to avoid the dangers of friendly fire. He explained that that practice took place after one of their members had been kidnapped, I believe. And then we heard and saw documents indicating that from the 15th of April in 1999, ribbons were worn once again. But I suggest to you that if the logic of wearing ribbons is to avoid friendly fire and to identify yourselves and you're doing that in July 1998, that when the war starts in March and you're engaged in these anti-terrorist operations from before the beginning of the war on the 24th of March, the logic still pertains and there's no reason to believe that they didn't continue to wear ribbons. The fact that we don't have a document or a chart showing the schedule for which colour ribbons to wear on which days prior to April 15th does not negate the wearing of ribbons. And we have eye-witness testimony from victims in the village who say that the forces that came to their villages and committed the crimes were wearing ribbons. And related to his discussion about the evidence of Witness Sali hu at page 84, line 9, yesterday Mr. Lukic said in a statement Witness Salihu explains that he was taken prisoner on the 20th of September, 1999, I don't know if that's what he said but that's what's recorded in the transcript and that can't be right. His statement says it was the 29th of April. Your Honours, with that I only want to refer to Mr. Ackerman's old saw, at the end of his remarks he talked about the young prosecutor and the old crusty judge who told her at the conclusion of her case that dog won't hunt. We say that in this case, our Prosecution case is a dog that will hunt and indeed it's baying at the base of the tree of which these six accused are perched. We ask you to find them all guilty. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I do, and I'll be brief. I'll respond in turn to the points made by Mr. Hannis in the order he made them. First on the issue of the Supreme Command we would just redirect the Chamber to our final brief, paragraphs 62 to 116 and our previous submissions, and of course we do rely upon, as Mr. Hannis encouraged you to do, Mr. Milutinovic's interview, 604, on Supreme Command as well as the numerous VJ officers including Prosecution Exhibit -- Witness General Vasiljevic and the other members of the staff of the Supreme Command who testified on the issue. We note as well at paragraph 115 of our brief that there is seven or eight other members of the staff of the Supreme Command who are not questioned by the Prosecutor on this point and we say that's a matter worthy of comment which we make at paragraph 115. And the last point is that the Prosecutor remains silent in relation to 3D670, the subordination order of the 18th of April, 1999, and the conclusions of the VSO of the 4th of October, 1998, which we say goes to the heart of the issue. The second point I wish to make was in relation to the question you had for me, Judge Bonomy, on whether or not the staff of the Supreme Command had discretion or whether or not it implemented strictly the orders of the supreme commander. And there we refer you to paragraph 103 of our final submissions. There we have the evidence of Gajic and Curcin, who clearly state that every day, in the morning, General Ojdanic met with President Milosevic and the commander commanded the army through his staff, that is to say that the staff implemented the orders of its commander, paragraph 103 of our brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The third point was the wartime decree on ID cards. We agree with the Prosecutor that there are innocent explanations to this, as he stated. And on the dates involved we do direct you to 1D144, which contains the draft of that decree, the letter from Professor Markovic, the deputy prime minister, to Mr. Milutinovic. The draft decree is dated the 31st of March, 1999, and that draft decree was sent to Mr. Milutinovic for signature on the 6th of April, 1999, and according to P993, the Official Gazette, it came into force on the 7th of April, 1999. The evidence of Professor Markovic on re-examination is transcript 13626 to 13628. There he explained that the draft decree of the 31st of March would have been prepared within the Ministry of the Interior, it would have been sent to Mr. Milutinovic on the 6th of April following the government meeting, and it came into force on the 7th of April with its publication in the Official Gazette. The fourth point I wish to make is in regards to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure I've completely grasped that. Are you saying that a mistake in date was put on it and it was signed at the later date?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Official Gazette is the 7th of April, but the text of the decree says the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Albeit it was sent, you say, on the face of a document on the 6th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But we say there's no problem with the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That still doesn't explain why it continues to have the date the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The 31st of March is the date the decree was actually drafted, the draft of that decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: If you look at 1D144, and I invite you to peruse the original, the B/C/S, in the top right-hand corner is the word "predlog," p-r-e-d-l-o-g, which hasn't made it into the English translation, we noted this morning, but that word means "draft" in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the Official Gazette contain any reference to the 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Official Gazette text of the decree does say 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, we constantly here are having to alter documents because when they're signed a day has passed or a few days have passed and you make sure that the one you sign has the date of signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, you had in the witness box the deputy prime minister who explained the circumstances and he said part of the problem is likely the chaos of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The ...

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The next point I wish to address briefly is the -- Mr. Hannis's comments about the investigations which took place in late 1998 and 1999. The point there that we were making is that it was a legitimate position for the domestic authorities, including Dr. Dunjic and his colleagues, as well as the international forensic people from Finland to investigate those matters. The next point is the evidence around Ambassador Petritsch's testimony on bombing and massacres. The evidence is clearly set out in our brief, but in response to what Mr. Hannis said we know that Mr. Petritsch has no recollection that Mr. Milutinovic actually uttered these words. Petritsch testified that Mr. Kickert prepared the memo, and at transcript 11239, I believe it's 239 and not 231, Mr. Kickert said that Petritsch must have added the reference to bombing and massacres. So there's even confusion on this point of who prepared the memo, who put the words in, which we say is further evidence of the unreliability of this memo. The next point I wish to make is in relation to P2166, the purported minutes of the inter-departmental staff. I refer you to paragraphs 176-178 of our brief. And you recall that when this document was first tendered in evidence during the testimony of Vasiljevic we objected. And, Your Honour, you asked me whether our position is whether it's a clever forgery and the answer to the question is: Yes. Now, four witnesses have testified in relation to that document, four of whom were present on the 29th of October. That's General Dimitrijevic, Mr. Matkovic, Mr. Minic, and Mr. Andjelkovic. As we suggest in our brief, they cast serious doubt on the authenticity and reliability of P2166. And as a matter of law I would direct the Chamber to the Trial Chamber judgement in the Prosecutor versus Delalic, 18 November 1998, IT-96-21, paragraph 704, and there the Chamber sets out the law we say on the distinctions to be made between the admissibility of an exhibit and its probative value and the weight that should be accorded an unauthenticated document. In this case we say you should give no weight to P2166. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "clever forgery," do you rule out Susic as having any part in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the evidence is that Susic was not taking notes at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, indeed, but the document bears to be his document, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: On the face of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that you don't have to prove anything, Mr. O'Sullivan, but it does help if one can take the criticism all the way. But you go part of the way really; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No. I say that the burden is on the Prosecutor to convince you and he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: -- can't do it because the four people who testified told you otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And I will conclude at this point and on behalf of Mr. Zecevic and I, we would like to publicly acknowledge the tireless work and dedication of our Defence team, in particular our case manager Mr. Srdjan Mujanovic, and our legal assistant; Ms. Deirdre Montgomery, who worked primarily here in The Hague; as well as our team back in Belgrade Ms. Jelena Kuveljic-Dimitric; Ms. Mima Kovacevic; and Mr. Dragan Bacanovic. And finally, it's been a pleasure for me to work with Mr. Zecevic and an honour for me to appear before you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila, do you have rebuttal -- sorry, rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to enumerate, one, two, three, four, that's how we'll get through it the quickest. The Prosecutor determines the beginning of the work of the Joint Command on the basis of a document P1317. That document contains the termination of the work of the Joint Command and handing over the military documents as well. The Prosecutor uses the exhibit just like a smorgasbord for breakfast, you take what you want and leave the rest. So either the document is a good one or it isn't. They take General Vasiljevic as proof and evidence that the Joint Command ceased to work on that date. General Vasiljevic expressly says that he knows about the Joint Command for 1998 because he was informed by General Stojanovic. As for 1999 he has absolutely no idea at all, doesn't know about it at all, knows nothing about the composition. At the meeting there was a minimum of 15 people. He does not say who those 15 people were, he doesn't claim that they were the Joint Command, and he says in a notebook, this is what he writes, that it was a meeting in PRK, in the PRK, not the Joint Command, and that he doesn't know what Sainovic did there. Let me remind you that nobody said that it was a Joint Command meeting of all the people who were the participants at the meeting. Number two, with respect to Djakovic, the Prosecutor states that I said arbitrarily that when the meetings were held of the so-called Joint Command without the presence of Djakovic that no notes were kept, no records were kept, because there's no evidence that any such meetings were ever held. I would like to ask the Court to look at the Djakovic testimony on page 26383 which speaks about a number of such meetings, numerous such meetings, which were held, and since he wasn't there, there were no records. Let me remind you also of all the other things that speak about daily meetings. Point three, according to the Prosecutor, General Dimitrijevic lied before this Trial Chamber now, he lied now, and when he talked to Crosland they say he had no reason to lie. So that what the Prosecutor is doing is presenting a claim and then he doesn't tie himself in trying to prove the grounds for which he says that. Now I'm saying the opposite, that General Dimitrijevic, old and infirm as he is, ten years on, a retired person, a pensioner, has no reason to lie now, whereas he might have had a reason then and that is no empty claim because then I'd be the same as the Prosecutor. But what I'm going to provide you with proof and evidence. Take a look at the telegram, for example, of Witness Crosland, it is Exhibit P684, paragraph 5. There Crosland has doubts about General Dimitrijevic's words. Perhaps he wasn't telling the truth to justify himself for some reason, and then General Dimitrijevic perhaps has reason not to tell the truth and justify himself with respect to the events that took place then. But what reason would he have for doing something like that now, for saying something like that now? You know, to insult somebody of that calibre and standing and of that age, saying that he's not telling the truth, isn't the nicest and fairest thing that you can do. Provide evidence, go ahead. Then the Prosecutor correctly quotes what General Dimitrijevic said with respect to Pavkovic and the Joint Command. Now suddenly he likes certain portions, and from there I conclude that General Dimitrijevic doesn't seem to be quite unimportant. So where it suits the Prosecutor he says that he's telling the truth. Now, how does he explain and interpret this? Look at the whole sense of the testimony of what was stated because you can't just extract excerpts. General Dimitrijevic constantly claims that Pavkovic invented this Joint Command to justify the bad way in which he functioned and worked, and in that respect he mentions the document that my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan brought up a minute ago that he thought up this inter-departmental staff which was called the Joint Command and he questions and challenges ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- P2166 and P1317, Sakic's letter that he mentioned a moment ago because he claims it was written under Pavkovic's influence so that this Joint Command which he invented could be shoved into Milosevic's square. Let me repeat, we're dealing here with directness here, but that the Prosecutor is trying to lead the Trial Chamber to ignore the two years of bloody warfare that went on. I don't know what we were doing here otherwise. Point four, point four, the Prosecutor says that the Defence claims that Sainovic only spoke ten times at meetings of the alleged Joint Command. That's not what I said, Mr. Prosecutor. All I said was this: That ten sentences uttered by Sainovic, ten times he took the floor, this was extracted because it had some sort of command character or resembled some sort of command character whereas nothing else suited you. That's what I said. And that I don't know arithmetic, I agree with Mr. Hannis there, I studied something else but I never got far from the multiplications table. Point five, with respect to the defence of inhabited areas, P2086, the Prosecution mentions P1064 as proof and evidence that the units of the federal Ministry of Defence were resubordinated to MUP pursuant to a decision of the Joint Command. The Defence would like to indicate that this kind of resubordination never took place of the conscripts, first of all, because in P1044 -- 64 it is not units that are referred to, it's conscripts that are referred to, individuals therefore, and that was never agreed because the RPOs were formed soon afterwards and it's quite obvious that in 1999 there was no resubordination of units of the federal Ministry of the Interior [as translated] to MUP, no evidence and proof has been provided. Odalovic and Andjelkovic were here, they were commanders of the civilian protection system and from their testimony it is impossible -- there's been a mistake. I was talking about resubordination of units of the federal Ministry of Defence, not the interior but defence, to MUP. As I say, we heard Odalovic and Andjelkovic here, their testimonies, they were commanders of the civilian defence, and from their testimony it is impossible to draw the conclusion that they were subordinated to the MUP, as the Prosecutor's interpreting P1064. Now where have we got to? Ah, yes, point six. I'm worried again because when the Prosecutor speaks about Sainovic he uses Pavkovic's interview as proof of the existence of a Joint Command, where we agreed that that is something that cannot be stated and doesn't follow. The Prosecutor says that Pavkovic took reports to Sainovic and the source? P2060, paragraph 62, where it says, that's Vasiljevic's statement, where it says that in -- yes, it is P2600, 2600 is the correct number of that exhibit, paragraph 62 where it says that Pavkovic said to Ojdanic that he had told Sainovic that he had seen the Skorpions in Prolom Banja. First, it doesn't stand that Pavkovic reported Sainovic and had this duty to inform. He might have met him and told him that way. Secondly, Prolom Banja, shall we understand this once and for all, it's not on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and if it's not in Kosovo and Metohija, then what has that to do with the Joint Command at all? Something that isn't on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The third point, from one sentence which stands in General Vasiljevic's statement where it is recounted -- where Pavkovic allegedly said -- Sainovic draws the conclusion that Pavkovic -- I apologise. From one sentence that can be found in Vasiljevic's statement where he recounts what Pavkovic allegedly said, Sainovic draws the conclusion that Pavkovic is responding to Sainovic and is submitting a report to him from one sentence. Now, you can't draw a conclusion on the basis of one sentence like that. There are combat reports, orders, hundreds of other exhibits that the Prosecution and Defence used to see who Pavkovic reported to and informed and who he was receiving orders from. So one sentence has been extracted and juxtaposed to hundreds of combat documents of indisputable authenticity, let alone the fact that they didn't go a step further. How do I know whether Pavkovic actually said that to Sainovic? Because there are different documents by Pavkovic where we find that that was not the case. Point seven, the Prosecutor mentions another exhibit, P1435 and P1439, and he refers to page 29 and says that this is proof and evidence that the Joint Command issues orders. The Prosecutor, however, is ignoring the substance of those documents and the substance is this, that regardless of what anybody said or asked for, as the Prosecutor said ordered, the sovereign decision lay in the hands of the commander of the 3rd Army. He is the person who makes the decisions, who decides. The commander of the 3rd Army, let me remind you, forbade the forming of units for rapid intervention and the deployment of helicopters MiG 8, regardless of what anybody else said at the meeting of that so-called Joint Command. A rapid intervention unit mentioned in these exhibits were never formed and helicopters were never used as was proposed, as was put forward. The substance of the matter is this, what was stated at the meetings of this Joint Command influences the situation on the ground or not, how does it influence it or not, and this is proof and evidence precisely that the Joint Command represented none other than a debating club because matters stood as the commander of the 3rd Army ordered. And I remind you of what I said yesterday with respect to what Mr. Ackerman said, that when the commander of the 3rd Army said that something should cease to exist, then the documents were handed over to Slobodan Milosevic's cabinet or offices. And that's completely in keeping with 4D91 and in keeping with the testimony of General Simic and Djakovic. Therefore, Judge Chowhan rightly asked the Prosecutor to explain what the Joint Command was in 1999. There is no reasonable or meaningful explanation on the part of the Prosecution and the Defence claims once again that 1998 is not the same as the year 1999, they are two different years, and regardless of what went on in 1998 you must prove what went on in 1999. The difference is a war and the difference is NATO and analogies in criminal law is something that is absolutely not allowed. Now I'm going to say one more thing and that is this. I heard Mr. Hannis raising his voice for the first time today and when did he raise it, when he was talking about the Joint Command. How can we on the basis of all this evidence, et cetera, et cetera, and then the Court and then the Trial Chamber, and then Mr. Hannis, and so on and so forth? So Cicero, the Greek slave went down in history, Cicero prepared his speeches and this -- the Greek slave prepared evidence for him and whenever there was proof and evidence he would write a footnote; when there was no proof and evidence he would put a little note and say we're very low on evidence here so just raise your voice, raise the tone, and it seems that Mr. Hannis went to this same school of thinking because what is he offering, what is he offering up? There's -- I claim that that is so because I say so. Now, if the facts speak differently, then woe betide the facts. Now, I hope this kind of philosophy won't pass muster with you. Now, the basic question I raised and Judge Chowhan raised is did a Joint Command exist in 1999 led by Nikola Sainovic? Show me the proof, show me the evidence, I said that in 98 bis and I'm repeating that now. Show me the proof, let's see the proof and evidence, and instead of that, all I received was a raised tone or a louder voice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One matter, Mr. Fila, before you sit down, page 64, at the beginning of that page you deal with origins of the Joint Command and then you refer to the document my colleague Mr. O'Sullivan brought up a minute ago and then there's a gap when you confer and then you refer to P2166 and P1317, Sakic's letter that he mentioned a moment ago. What is it you're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to 2166 the way General Dimitrijevic explains it and Mr. O'Sullivan spoke about this, and the rest is a letter from the federal Ministry of Justice from which the Prosecutor extracted only the beginning, that the Joint Command began and the rest of the letter seems to be non-existent in his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So Sakic's letter is the letter in answer to the RFA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I offered you another letter but you didn't accept it. It was better, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, do you have rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, several points raised by Mr. Hannis today. On pages 4 and 5 of today's transcript Mr. Hannis referred to your question on a certain amount of discretion that the supreme staff might have had in its work and he referred to the testimony of General Curcin. It is our assertion, Your Honours, that these references which Mr. Hannis made do not constitute a response to your question. They are an addendum to paragraph 232 of Ojdanic's letter, speaking of a certain amount of autonomy and discretion of the level of command. I will draw your attention to transcript pages, General Radinovic's testimony, 17247, line 22, to 17251, where he explained the role of the Supreme Command Staff in relation to the supreme commander and in relation to the commanders of the strategic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what date was that evidence given?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 18th of October, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're talking about the interrelations between the Supreme Command Staff, we come -- and others, we come to the other topic raised by Mr. Hannis today and that is a document entitled: "Suggestions and relations of General Ojdanic towards the operation in Rugovska Klisura." Mr. Hannis devoted a significant part of his presentation to this topic. He spoke about the relations of General Ojdanic and others command over the Pristina Corps command, over the 2nd Army, and so on. And we assert that Mr. Hannis is wrong when he states that the key for the issuing of this document is the fact that the 2nd Army was involved in this operation, and I'll tell you why. Because the suggestion was issued on the 17th of April and the order of the Joint Command on the 15th of April, two days previously. For there to be coordination between the 2nd Army and the 3rd Army the order on coordination would have had to be issued before that. I will also draw your attention to a document we did not mention in our brief but which we dealt with. It has to do with the Joint Command and the suggestion document in paragraphs 208 and 204. The document I wish to mention now is 4D412 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 420.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it's report by the 3rd Army to the Supreme Command Staff where in paragraph 1 it is clearly stated. 4D420, I suggest we look at it perhaps. It is clearly stated here that the order for the operation was issued by the supreme commander, that as early as on the 12th of April. And, Your Honours, this fits in and it confirms our case that the Supreme Command Staff as the expert staff organ formulated the orders issued by the supreme commander. In addition to this, in the same document on, or rather, in point 2, I don't know whether it's in e-court or not, there is reference to the ultimate fate of this suggestions document. The suggestions never reached their destination for the reasons mentioned here, General Pavkovic was absent at his command post and so on and so forth. So no wonder that this document is mentioned again in the order of the 20th of April when coordination is being done again for the same operation. I also wish to draw your attention to the footnotes, or rather, to the testimony of General Radinovic in connection with this topic on pages 17335 and 17335 of the transcript and that's the 19th of October, 2007 -- 17335 and 17336. May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to the next topic raised by Mr. Hannis, and that is the statements of General Ojdanic in the course of 1997 and 1998. Mr. Hannis says that subsequently General Ojdanic changed his purpose. There is no evidence to show that General Ojdanic changed his standpoints. There is evidence to show that in early 1999 the conditions in which General Ojdanic was operating changed, and we spoke about these conditions sufficiently in our letter. They include the growth of the KLA and the external threat of NATO aggression. The next topic raised by Mr. Hannis was knowledge of possible crimes committed in 1998, and he gives as an example Gornje Obrinje and he makes a link between this and General Ojdanic. I wish to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that in at least one military document, and that's P1440 in point 2, it says what the military organs knew had happened or not happened in Gornje Obrinje and this would be the basis of any knowledge that General Ojdanic might have had, if he indeed did have any knowledge. As regards the general knowledge gleaned from the media and common knowledge, in my view the Court should be extremely cautious. Today we had a typical example of this showing what publication in the media means. Mr. Hannis said that he learned relatively late about when the indictment in this case was published. I have an information sheet for every visitor entering this Tribunal and it says on the 27th of May, the Prosecutor Louise Arbour published the indictment. I'm saying this not because it's evidence but because sometimes even persons as highly interested as Mr. Hannis was in this case or General Ojdanic in the Gornje Obrinje case might pass someone by without being noticed. The next topic I wish to raise is the movement of the population, and here Mr. Hannis said, referring to the collegium of the 9th of April, that General Gajic envisaged what would happen with the refugees. But he omitted to mention that in our letter in paragraph 263, point G -- [In English] I'm sorry, in our brief, it should be. [Interpretation] In our closing brief in paragraph 263 from point G to J we enumerated the previous knowledge and discussion concerning refugees. So General Gajic wasn't talking about this as something that would happen in the future. This had already been discussed. So what my learned friend did was misinterpret General Gajic's statements at the meeting of the 9th of April. The next topic is the establishing of the commission on the 17th of May at the meeting. Mr. Hannis said that this was in fact a suggestion. He said that the commission was to be formed in order to hush up what had happened and this had to do with what happened sixth months previously concerning the wire-tapping, listening in to the army. This would mean that the setting up of any sort of commission constituted an attempt to hush things up. And secondly, if General Ojdanic really wanted to put a stop to this issue and to have it end at the establishing of the Joint Commission, why then did he send Generals Vasiljevic and Gajic out into the field? Why did he form his own group to go out into the field and conduct an investigation? Why did he order on the 7th of July that priority should be given to war crimes? [In English] I'm sorry, it should be 7th June. [Interpretation] Why did he order that actions where international humanitarian law had been violated should be given priority? I also wish to mention that this is completely contrary to the impression and testimonies of Generals Gajic, Vasiljevic, and Farkas before this Tribunal; they were direct participants of the meetings on the 16th and 17th of May, and General Dimitrijevic who in his general assessment of General Ojdanic said that General Ojdanic wanted to learn the truth. Now that we're mentioning witnesses, Mr. Hannis said he didn't expect us to call witnesses who would confirm there was a plan, but it wasn't only our witnesses. Our witnesses, in fact, only confirmed what Mr. Hannis's witnesses had said, what Vasiljevic, Dimitrijevic, Loncar, and Pesic had said, that there was never a plan. And finally, Your Honours, on my own behalf and on behalf of Mr. Sepenuk, I wish to thank all those who worked with us over the past six years, our case managers, Ms. Zivkovic, Mr. Ivanovic, the legal part of our team, Mr. Selezan, Ms. Janjic, Mr. Brent Hicks, Mr. Russell Hopkins, and Mr. Peter Robinson, and Ms. Danijela Borjektarevic; to our investigators, Ilija Isak, and Ratko Djukanovic; and I also wish to thank Mr. Sepenuk for his cooperation. Your Honours, it was an honour to defend General Ojdanic before this Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend Mr. Hannis spoke today about General Ojdanic omitting to take disciplinary measures or punish my client, and he referred to General Dimitrijevic's testimony who allegedly said that General Perisic initiated these proceedings. But as my client had been promoted, all this got lost somewhere. So in connection with that, I wish to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to some exhibits and a chronology of events and of General Perisic's and Dimitrijevic's actions in 1998; and then on the basis of this, I wish to -- and on the basis of the exhibits in this case, Your Honours may decide what really happened. In 1D760, Exhibit 1D760, these are stenographic notes from the 5th Session of the Supreme Defence Council. On page 9, paragraph 4 of the English version General Perisic says in relation to the frequently repeated claim that he was in favour of declaring a state of emergency, whereas my client and some others were opposed to this. He says the following. He's saying that: "The KLA's on the increase, that terrorism is on the increase, and he says everything should be done to prevent this by political negotiations. If it is not prevented, then we will have to engage the peacetime army according to the measure of escalation and if there is a threat of aggression from outside we will have to go for mobilisation." So General Perisic here is drawing a clear distinction between external aggression and dealing with the terrorists, the KLA, as an internal enemy, so to say. At that same meeting, and that's the same exhibit, page 14 in English, in the Serbian language it's page 15, there is mention of some staffing issues and General Perisic is speaking again and he proposes the following, that Slobodan Antonic should become deputy commander of the Pristina Corps so that that could be -- that part of the job could be strengthened with a very able man who had certain wartime experience so that one of them, and I'm adding here now, General Lazarevic was already the Chief of Staff and the deputy corps commander, so General Perisic is proposing another deputy for General Pavkovic so that one of them, either Antonic or Lazarevic, could always be where the focus of combat actions were or on the terrain while the other could be dealing with business in the command. And that's the 9th of June, Your Honours, and General Perisic is the one saying this. Furthermore -- in 1998, that is. Furthermore, in chronological order on the 18th of June, that's Exhibit 4D139, and this is a commendation by General Perisic for General Pavkovic as a good soldier and supreme professional, and one can say, well, he wasn't the only one who received this, but if they had something against him and if my client was acting contrary to the way he should have behaved, then there was no reason for him to be commended, especially commended. Furthermore, my learned friend Mr. Hannis, and I don't have the precise reference because I'm on my own, I had to do something else, but he said that it was up to the General Staff to issue a directive as the basic document and then the lower levels, armies and corps, would draw up other documents for specific actions. Well, on the 28th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down, the interpreter did not catch all the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, the interpreter's having difficulty keeping up with your pace. Can you give these numbers again. The interpretation breaks off at "on the 28th ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. On the 28th of July, 1998, the directive of General Perisic which is Exhibit Number 4D137 was issued. After that we have an order by General Samardzic three days later but let's leave that to one side for the time being. After that General Perisic tours the units in Kosovo, on the 13th of August, and that is Exhibit 4D143, that is to say General Perisic issues oral orders at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica and says - and I don't want to repeat this because we've already dealt with it - when he went back to Belgrade three days later on the 16th of August he issues a new order and that is Exhibit 4D416. One of the points in that order states as follows: Prevent the Siptar terrorist forces from overflowing into the area of Raska, the south Morava area, and another area and General Mladenovic testified about that, Tomislav Mladenovic, so those three areas are outside of Kosovo and Metohija. Now, I'm wondering how is it possible for General Perisic to order -- issue this order to General Samardzic and then General Samardzic -- General Pavkovic to perform that assignment, whereas those three geographic wholes, geographic areas, are, in fact, outside of Kosovo and Metohija. And that's precisely what he's ordering, not in the border belt or whatever other area that the Prosecution claims. As far as General Perisic is concerned, just two more points that I'd like to focus on, could you look at Exhibit 3D757, focus your attention on that, it's an expose by General Perisic, a very long one, extensive one, so under Roman numeral II points 1 to 6 General Perisic sets out the involvement and deployment of the Army of Yugoslavia thus far. That's the 1st of October, and after that you have Exhibit 3D697 of the 2nd of October which is an analysis of the 3rd Army about what was done during the three or four previous months. Now, why have I said all this? Your Honours, I think that from these exhibits, the ones that I've just mentioned, it follows quite clearly that General Perisic was in favour of the deployment of the army, he was conscious of all the actions and everything else, and that he had knowledge about what the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army were doing in the previous period and that everything was done, all this was done on the basis of his directive and orders from the General Staff. As far as General Dimitrijevic is concerned, we deal with this in several paragraphs of our final brief, we discuss his testimony, and let me just add this to what I've already said. During my cross-examination General Dimitrijevic said that he did not know of a single specific action performed by Pavkovic outside General Vasiljevic's knowledge. Sepenuk -- Mr. Sepenuk said in part of his presentation that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 78, line 16, instead of Mr. -- General Vasiljevic, it should be General Samardzic, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I apologise once again for speaking so quickly. My colleague Mr. Sepenuk in his closing arguments said that the only two cases in which General Dimitrijevic was against something at the beginning was in Podujevo and Racak; however, those two cases I think we have dealt with and seen that the army was not involved in any way on the basis of the exhibits that were presented, that the army did not violate the October Agreements. So except for those two incidents, General Dimitrijevic did not say anything else in his testimony against my client, and we have supporting material to prove that. Now, as far as bringing in the units to Kosovo and Metohija I think that Mr. Hannis had in mind there after the OSCE mission the -- Mr. Hannis said that my client even without the knowledge of the General Staff brought in units to Kosovo. I think that Mr. Ackerman, my learned friend, addressed this, I don't think that is correct, so please look at exhibits P1947 and P1948, and they are illustrative of the situation. Now, as far as reporting is concerned, Mr. Hannis said that Witness Farkas said during his testimony about the blockage -- well, I think that Mr. Ackerman was right [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Aleksic, we've lost the interpretation. There was astonishment I think when you said that you thought Mr. Ackerman was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A moment, the interpreter still has not recovered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that what is much more important and something that Mr. Ackerman mentioned was part of the testimony of General Farkas and Vasiljevic and Gajic, that after all the inspections had been carried out, as Vojinovic sent them to establish, that they established that 95 per cent of the cases were investigated in fact and that's the point of that testimony. And in addition to that, I think that during the presentation of evidence we showed that at least two or three other systems of reporting existed which were independent of General Pavkovic, and you can see that evidenced in 4D -- just a moment, please, let me find the number, 4D499, which is the statement by Colonel Velimir Obradovic. And just briefly, a few words on two points. Today my colleague Mr. Hannis on page 43, lines 7 onwards, 7 to 9, said that the army took part in digging up and examining corpses in Izbica. That is not correct, and in connection with that take a look at Gordana Tomasevic's testimony. Her statement is P2490, paragraph 30, in which she says that the instructions were given for that location from the investigating judge of the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica and so on and so forth. She spoke about that in great detail and raised some of the problems in that regard. But quite obviously it was the civilian court and not a military court that ordered this exhumation and the examination of those bodies. As far as disclosure is concerned of the indictment against Milosevic, my colleague Mr. Visnjic talked about that. We arrived at that information during our work on the final brief, so that's the reason why we did not raise that as an argument earlier. And finally with respect to the existence of -- alleged existence of the Joint Command in 1999, my learned friend Mr. Hannis used an interview given by my client to the Prosecution, to the OTP, P949, but on pages 113 and 114 General Pavkovic says the following: "From the beginning of the ground campaign we met once or twice but not with those people present." And on page 114 he goes on to say the following: "It was no official meeting. We just happened to meet, quite simply, because we were in a position to bump into each other and be at the same place at the same time." And in one of those meetings General Djakovic speaks about this in his testimony and says that that was on the 19th of April in some bank building and that is to be found on transcript page -- just a moment, please, I need a moment to find it, 26494 to 26496. But that was a meeting about the resubordination of the MUP which they held with the officers of the MUP, of course without the presence of anybody else, just the military and police officials. Your Honours, that would be it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Just one transcript matter. Page 81, line 5, I think you said from the beginning of the Grom campaign; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the NATO campaign. It seems just campaign was recorded, so that must be my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, the quotation you gave is from the beginning of the ground campaign, and that's accurate, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant the transcript of the interview of my client, P949, it just says from the beginning of the campaign there, that's what I was referring to, not this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Hannis, in responding with respect to our closing arguments, he began by showing P1723 or mentioning 1723, and by that exhibit in actual fact he rounded off that area. It is the report of the 24th of May, and Mr. Hannis pointed out to the Trial Chamber some of the errors and inexactitudes with respect to the way in which this document was registered. And I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that many exhibits in this case and witnesses told us that the command of the Pristina Corps during the bombing very frequently would relocate from one place to another, from one day to the next, which meant that the documents followed them too and the log-books, et cetera. And just this possible mistake or the lack of logics in the way this was logged and recorded cannot be proof and evidence that this was something that did not happen, especially if we bear in mind that General Lazarevic did testify about this document and said that he had compiled it on the basis of certain information that he had from the 37th Brigade and that in that sense he sent a commission to examine the situation. These statements by General Lazarevic were borne out by Witness Radojko Stefanovic, who together with officer Paprica went to the 37th Motorised Brigade to try and establish what the situation was, what it was all about, and Momir Stojanovic, a Defence witness, and he was a security chief. So from this testimony we can see that it was an authentic piece of evidence and an authentic exhibit. Mr. Hannis began with that exhibit and then ended by saying that in addition -- beside the fact that the general on the 24th of May wrote the document, that nothing further was -- no further steps were taken by him. Well, General Lazarevic was a corps commander, he was the commander of the army, an army commander, so not by law or by the chain of command did he have any power and authority vis-a-vis MUP members. Moreover, he wasn't in -- at a strategic level for him to be able to do anything other than inform his superior commander. And general -- that is precisely what General Lazarevic did, with the information that he received, checked out or not, he informed his superior commander about that. The second point is this, my learned friend speaks about Exhibit P1428, and that is the action of Slup and Voksa. I would like -- and the order for that action was signed by General Lazarevic. I would like to point out to the Trial Chamber that they should look at paragraphs 542 to 575 carefully, that is to say paragraphs in our final brief, where you can clearly see the chronology in which these tasks were issued. So as for this order we can see exactly that it was issued, that it was ordered, within the frameworks of the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia. I've already said once when Mr. Hannis put something to a witness and he reacted and said that in P1468 it did not state that General Lazarevic would be in charge and command the operation, what it says that General Lazarevic might or could be put in charge of this operation. And that's something that General Pavkovic said at a meeting of the Joint Command and I still claim the so-called, alleged Joint Command of course, where we see that as to the action that was decided upon in the 3rd Army he was just informing the meeting about that. He was just providing information and saying that that action could be commanded by General Lazarevic before the action went ahead. However, I'd like to point out to the Trial Chamber the testimony of General Lazarevic and Goran Jevtovic's testimony, who at the time was the operative at the forward command post, where we can clearly see that General Lazarevic was at the border when this action was actually taking place. And let me say, even had he been in command of this action, if he had commanded and led this action, so what? What then? The action took place within the border belt, the action led to no casualties or crimes, and General Lazarevic as the Chief of Staff at the forward command post was authorised by law to lead the action. So what does the Prosecution thesis and case prove in this respect, even if it were correct that he was in command of the action? And we claim everything that we've indicated to you so far. We've already stated what we claim. As regards Exhibit 5D175, my learned friend Mr. Hannis repeats that there is a strange discrepancy between the date and the log-book. Let me repeat that this was happening in a state of wartime chaos in early April, the very beginning of fierce NATO air-strikes, the command was relocating, and this is a more logical explanation for a discrepancy in dates than it would be to assume that then, on the 6th of April, General Lazarevic, as the commander of the Pristina Corps, ordered the 3rd Army which sent the order on down the chain of command to the staff of the Supreme Command. Is that a logical supposition? Analyse the directive, the order, the orders and you'll see what the sequence of events actually was. My colleague -- my learned friend Mr. Hannis speaks of witness Nike Peraj and his assertion that he saw General Lazarevic one day towards the end of April in Djakovica. And now faced with all the Defence arguments my learned friend Mr. Hannis says, no, that was on the 29th of April in the context of a broader action, although the Reka action was already finished. Your Honours, I invite you to look at the context of Nike Peraj's statement, to look at what happened immediately prior to his seeing General Lazarevic and immediately after his having seen him. He says that after he saw him on the 28th in the morning and received permission he went to Osa Hilja to see how the Reka action was progressing. So he could not have been mistaken as regards the 29th of April. His testimony has to be viewed in the context of everything he said, and you will see that there's no possibility that this was the 29th of April. I refer you to paragraphs 465 to 468 of our closing brief, our final brief, where we analyse the testimony of Nike Peraj. On the 29th of April, that is, the Reka action was already finished and there's no possibility that the sequence of events mentioned by Peraj could have taken place on that day. In addition to this, Your Honours, we repeat that on the 29th of April General Lazarevic was on the territory of the 125th Motorised Brigade, that's the Pec area, not the Djakovica area. And we have already explained that in the combat report of that brigade it says from 9.00 to 12.00. Minutes are not entered into combat reports. And General Zivanovic said here, testifying as a witness, that the place where General Lazarevic saw elements of the 37th at 9.00 a.m., it takes 15 or 20 minutes to reach his staff in Pec and we've already drawn your attention to this testimony. My learned friend Mr. Hannis in Exhibit 5D379, or rather, in connection with this exhibit he says, Yes, we see that on the 26th of April General Lazarevic did ask for a team to come because there was suspicion that soldiers were mixed up in some crimes, but he did nothing else subsequently. We have presented much evidence here, abundant evidence, and we quoted Witness Vasiljevic which shows that General Lazarevic's duties and authorities stopped there. I draw Your Honours' attention to two exhibits, one is Exhibit P2029, item 4, where as early as on the 1st of April General Lazarevic orders his units to form temporary units consisting of tried and tested selected men who would be included in the military police in order to assist in catching and identifying perpetrators of negative phenomena. In 5D365, items 3, 4, and 5, and that is an exhibit dated the 5th of April, General Lazarevic demanded from his subordinate units that unobstructed engagement and the safe works of military investigative and judicial organs should be provided for and that these orders were to be strictly complied with. On the 5th of April, before that, as soon as the military war courts were established General Lazarevic is ordering his units to make sure that the military investigative and judicial organs were able to do their work, and he invited the exhumation teams. What else could a military commander when his corps was attacked from outside and from within, what else could he do? If he invited the exhumation teams, if he asked his units to provide unhindered access and safe work to the investigative organs, what else was he supposed to do? Should he have gone and done the exhumations himself, dug up the graves himself? No, that was not his duty. He fulfilled his duty, as Witness Vasiljevic already testified. And furthermore, my learned friend Mr. Hannis said that our Defence did not prove that there was no resubordination and he says on the 20th to the 22nd of May Colonel Kotur issued an order from the forward command post for the Sekac action. We say that on the 20th, 21st, and 22nd of May that information sheet had not yet been compiled and the decision on resubordination, or rather, the order on resubordination had not been withdrawn, it was still in force. The Sekac action was being planned as a joint action of the army and the MUP, and as evidence to the contrary I draw Your Honours' attention to Exhibit 5D1382, that's a combat report of the 22nd of May, 1992 [as interpreted], from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps and in paragraph 2 on page 2 it says that control of the Sekac action Colonel Milan Kotur with the chief of the SUP of Djakovica on Suka Vogelj facility where there's an observation post. So on this document you can see there's no resubordination because Milan Kotur is in charge for the army and Kovacevic, the chief of the SUP is in charge for the MUP. Your Honours, in line 19 it says 22nd of May 1992. I said 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend Mr. Hannis referred to numerous exhibits we showed concerning the orders issued by General Lazarevic, showing his concern for the civilian population and that they should be taken care of. And my learned friend Mr. Hannis, if I understood him correctly, said, well, it doesn't say anything about what population this refers to. Had there been any intention of separating the population at least one of those orders would have said that it was the Serbian civilian population that had to be assisted, but here it just says civilian population. I draw Your Honours' attention to the testimony of Zoran Andjelkovic on transcript pages 14668 and 14669. He was shown Exhibit 5D412 which is a request by General Lazarevic that the interim Executive Council should assist civilians with food and medicines. When I asked whether he was familiar with the document, the witness confirmed that he was. When I asked him what civilian population it referred to he said the population from the town of Glogovac. When I asked him what the ethnic make-up in the town of Glogovac was, he said, Well, there are one or two Serb families; all the others are Albanians. There are numerous other pieces of evidence, numerous other exhibits, Your Honours, but our time is very short. But you can see from all this that assistance to the civilian population was intended for all civilians regardless of their ethnicity or their religious or national affiliation. And finally, Witness K-73 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, with respect, Mr. Bakrac, you've misunderstood the submission that Mr. Hannis made. He thought it was a point favourable to you that there was no reference to ethnicity in relation to the civilian population. His argument related thereafter to conduct, not the content of the document. However, we have your submissions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I did allow for the possibility that I misunderstood him. And as for subsequent actions, we dealt with this in our final brief and you will see that the reports of lower-ranking units showed what was done pursuant to these orders, for example, Exhibit 5D516 and other exhibits we referred to in our final brief. And my learned friend Mr. Hannis quoted Witness K-73. I won't go into his ethnic affiliation or other affiliations, so we need not move into private session, but I will just invite you to look at paragraphs 381 to 386 of our final brief where we analyse in detail his testimony. And I invite you to look at transcript -- the transcripts, pages 3412 to 3415, these are the transcript pages of his testimony. After what was quoted and presented to you by my learned friend Mr. Hannis you will see that with respect to his unit and the unit that participated alongside his, he stated in cross-examination that these were honourable men, that these were real soldiers who never violated anything, or rather, never committed an offence. So please look at these transcript pages and I ask you only for two or three minutes of your patience, because my colleague Mr. Cepic will address you briefly. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we could deal with that I think after the break, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you can assist us by giving some indication if you can of how long you might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be very brief. I wish to refer to the issue of whether there was any distinction drawn in providing humanitarian assistance to civilians, or rather, I wish to point out that there was no distinction drawn with respect to ethnicity as to humanitarian assistance. I wish to refer to 5D615, item 9 of this exhibit, which clearly shows that on that occasion assistance was provided to Albanians and all the other documents shown here show the same. The next issue I wish to talk about is the issue of Izbica which was mentioned by my learned friend Mr. Hannis, who said that the military judicial organs conducted an investigation in that area in connection with that incident, and I will refer to the testimony of Witness Bogunovic, 2518 and 2509 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 25108 and 25109 are the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he says that the necessary actions were undertaken by the MUP and this is in Exhibit 6D613. And the last topic I wish to refer to is the topic of the border belt. My learned friend Mr. Hannis showed a schematic here which was supposed to show that area, and I will refer to the testimony of Colonel Cucak, a Defence witness of General Ojdanic's Defence, who gave us a detailed explanation of this matter inter alia pointing out that the breadth of the border belt was not the same everywhere in all parts, that in some places it was considerably narrower than elsewhere. And his statements are supported by Exhibit 3D739, which is a map of the border belt in the southern part of the FRY. This is diametrically opposite to what we saw in the diagram or schematic drawing shown to us by my learned friend Mr. Hannis which shows the border belt for all of Kosovo and not just the border towards Albania and Macedonia. I wish to thank you again for your attention and that's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] First of all, we'd like to deal with -- well, I'll be giving transcript references. Today's transcript page 10, line 25, where Exhibit P2166 is mentioned and colleague Hannis today proposed, or rather, put that Colonel Susic probably had a report which was P1011 and he gained information from that about the number of ammunitions and men. And in our opinion this is yet further evidence, even if that theory were to be accepted, that it wasn't a minutes but a compilation. So Susic according to these assertions did not record the words of the speaker. This OTP position challenges the authenticity of P2166 as well. Page 14, line 14, what is proposed there by the Prosecutor is that the plan, the general plan or five-phase, five-stage plan was designed after a meeting of the 30th of May, 1998. That is not correct, it's not true. We have testimony from Milan Djakovic on page 25541 of the transcript where he says that his task was the task he was given -- he was given a task after the meeting of the 9th of June with Milosevic, the Supreme Defence Council meeting. Transcript page 20, Gornje Obrinje is mentioned, and linked to that we would just like to state and ask the Trial Chamber to look at Jan Kickert, a Prosecution witness, who explained in his testimony that there were several attempts to investigate the area, to conduct an investigation there but that that was impossible because of a strong KLA presence there who did not -- which did not allow access to the organs of Serbia to go on site and this was testified to by Danica -- Judge Danica Marinkovic as well. Transcript page 26, line 14 speaks about the confiscation of documents. The Defence claimed, opposed to what the OTP presented and Mr. Hannis said today, that not a single witness said, actually said that documents, ID documents, were personally seized from them at the border crossings, at Djeneral Jankovic, Cafa Prusit, and Globocica. They did mention -- some of them at least mentioned having seen, or rather, that somebody told them that their documents had been taken away from them. Everybody who testified in this court and had crossed over these three border crossings can be stated to be persons whose personal documents, ID documents, had not been confiscated. So we put the following question: What plan could there have been to seize documents at one border crossing, Vrbnica, without having confiscating them at other border crossings, and I think that the chief of border police at Vrbnica himself explained the situation at the border crossing sufficiently and he says that he left the documents there, that Albanian civilians were leaving behind documents, that they were in sacks and handed over to the international forces when they came in. Page 27, line 17 speaks about the departure of people from Pristina first of all linked to the trains. His Honour Judge Chowhan asked Mr. Hannis whether there were more or fewer trains and he was not given an answer to his question, but I'll tell you, Judge, there were 228 instead of 780 trains, which was the normal number of trains as testified to by Witness Bucaliu. So in the period after the bombing, after the start of the bombing, not on any single day were there ten trains, which was normal, just on one day during the bombings there were nine trains. There were some days where there were no trains, other days there were two trains, one or two trains, and so on and so forth. Now, on that same page, page 27, Kabashi's testimony is mentioned, who claimed that on a daily basis there were nine to 12 trains leaving. That is not correct, it's not true. And we can see that during -- we saw that during the proceedings. It was proved and shown that the log-book that Bucaliu brought with him here into court and which was Exhibit P1331 registered the passage of trains correctly and the Prosecution witness Bucaliu did state that and the Defence didn't challenge it. Otherwise, until the departure of the civilians, or rather, the departure of the civilians took place after the 28th and 29th of March when the centre of Pristina was bombed and the MUP building was hit, and once again when the centre of Pristina was hit on the 7th of April, when the post office building was hit. In those intervals we see the greatest departure of civilians from the town of Pristina itself. That's when most of the people left. And Mihajlovic testified to that, Mihajlo Mihajlovic -- no, his name is Milivoje, Milivoje Mihajlovic. His statement was 6D1530, paragraph 35, transcript page, page 29 of the transcript, and I'm moving on to another area, lines 14 to 21, it says what General Pavkovic reported on and subjects discussed at the Joint Command meetings. We would like to ask you to take a look at the dates in the notebooks and minutes of the meetings denoted as Joint Command ones. And as far as we've been able to check out so far, nothing was recorded about this at those meetings, nothing about the subjects that Pavkovic says were discussed. Now page 31 of the transcript, there was discussion about number 455-172, the entry there, and as far as we were able to check out in the operative log-book, that number does not deal with resubordination at all. Page 31, line 4 this time, discusses two documents, P1458 or another number that is used in these proceedings P1723. It is a document of the 24th of April and another document P1459 and the other number is P1724. Then we'd like to make the following comments. At that time there was control underway of the Pristina Corps by the Main Staff. Witness Simic claims that neither Lazarevic nor Pavlovic [as interpreted] said anything about the Pristina Corps control in the documents and that it doesn't exist in 3D692 either. Simic testified to that on transcript page 15674, lines 14 to 21. And we'd also like to add that not a single military witness for the Defence agreed with the contents of the letters which were presented and mentioned here. There's another document, P1725 dated the 4th of June, 1999, issued by the 3rd Army command which speaks about resolving the problem and nowhere in that document is it stated -- nowhere there can you see what is stated in the documents of the 24th and 25th, the previous documents, that is to say crimes committed by the MUP. Transcript page 43, line 16, the crossing of state borders, that's a subject Mr. Hannis referred to as well as my colleague Mr. Cepic on page 91, line 3. We would like to stress that the law governing border crossings and control in the border belt has nothing to do with the defence of the state border from a ground aggression and rules that apply in wartime. And we'd ask the Trial Chamber to look at P1007, page 136, paragraph 520 to 536, where mention is made of inhabited areas. On page 49, line 11, the Skorpions are mentioned, and we stressed this several times during the proceedings and we'd like to reiterate this, that nothing was known of the crimes of the Skorpions until the Slobodan Milosevic trial came about, when a video was shown to Obrad Stevanovic, I think it was. They were crimes committed by the Skorpions in Bosnia, however. The people who went to Kosovo weren't the same people who had been in the Skorpions in Bosnia before the war. Stoparic himself says that 50 per cent of those people who went to Kosovo had no combat experience at all. So 50 per cent of those people quite certainly had not been in Bosnia because they hadn't had any combat experience. Now, as far as the allegations of the Skorpion crimes as alleged by the Prosecution are concerned, Judge Bonomy rightly noted, and we'd like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the following pages, I think page 154 -- I just have to give a justification here. It is line [as interpreted] 51 of the transcript, line 7 where it says that my colleague Mr. Ivetic erroneously quoted Ms. Kravetz, and I can say that both Ivetic and Mr. Hannis are right because in the corrected transcript we saw that Kravetz was right -- Ms. Kravetz was right. However, in the transcript we had we received after the court proceedings, we couldn't see this section where she says that there was no KLA at Milosh Giliq Street number 157. So I accept that correction. Page 52, line 17, paragraph 228 of the Prosecution brief was discussed, where they claim that the Joint Command issued orders for joint actions and Lukic's role was, they say, to see to the plans passed by the Joint Command which included MUP units be put into practice and that he determined which units would participate. And as a source they quote Cvetic. Let us repeat again, Cvetic was not a member of the staff nor a member of the Joint Command, he never attended any Joint Command meetings either or meetings designated as such. He never explained where he got the information from, the information that the Prosecution refers to and information he clearly stated during his testimony. We say to you that that is not correct and that he could not have had that information in the first place. Page 53, line 12 refers to the fact that Vasiljevic said that the members of the JSO had 150 years of imprisonment when it was established -- JSO, when the JSO was established, and the fact that in 1999 Vasiljevic went back to the service and Dimitrijevic was retired. However, that was not the period that this addresses. It is the time when the JSO was founded, which is 1996 and not 1999. And at that time Vasiljevic was already a pensioner. At that time he had no official information whatsoever. At that same time Dimitrijevic had all the information relating to the military and security situation because he was the chief. Transcript page 54, line 21, the OTP here proposes that he -- even before the 15th of April, 1999, the police wore bands and was designated with bands and this was supported by Prosecution witnesses. They say that they were marked in 1998, had the markings in 1999 -- in 1998 and then that was the case when the war started as well. May we have in e-court now 6D237, please. What is the Prosecution asking the Trial Chamber? The Trial Chamber [as interpreted] is asking you once again to draw the following conclusions and inferences at the debit of the accused without in dubio pro reo. We say that every time you draw conclusions you must do so to the advantage of the accused. For us to facilitate your quest in this instance we're going to show you by looking at a few sentences that the assertions and claims made by the Prosecution are not the right ones and that you're not to draw those conclusions. The document is quite clear and I'm sure you'll agree with us that the document states quite the opposite to what the Prosecution claims and the first point is this. You will see that the document is dated the 13th of April, so not the beginning of the month, not the middle of the month, it's the 13th of April, that's the date. And what it says is the following. "We are forwarding armbands for policemen," so only at that point are they forwarding these armbands. They weren't thrown away, they were used non-stop. And it says: "... for their distribution in units." In the next paragraph it says: "We are forwarding the instructions on armbands for policemen in April 1999." It doesn't say the second half of April, it says "in April." These armbands should be used as of the 15th of April, 1990 [as interpreted] at 0001 hours. The armbands are to be worn as of, it doesn't say continue to be worn, it says that they should start to be worn as of the 15th of April, 1999. And one further explanation by our Defence and you'll weigh it up, it is linked to the term and body of the Joint Command. The body the Joint Command does not exist in the sense as explained by Mr. Hannis. Why was it called that? Well, it was called that, for example, because our client denoted it that way when he first talked to the OTP, he kept referring to this body as the so-called because according to him and according to us, meetings for an exchange of information cannot be called Joint Command. Line 20 and 21, it should read "so-called Joint Command," the term and the body of the so-called Joint Command. And I have one more point and for that one more point to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move to that, could you go back briefly to the document which is still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you go to page 3 of that, you'll see there's reference there to PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Those units apart from SUP members were also receiving those ribbons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
